item.title: Years after leaving Google Photos, the thing I miss most isn't what I expected
item.itunes:title: Years after leaving Google Photos, the thing I miss most isn't what I expected
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For years, Google Photos was the place where I kept my entire photo collection. It was one of those apps I rarely thought about because it simply worked in the background. Eventually, though, I decided I wanted a different approach and started looking for a way to manage my photos on my own terms. That led me to Immich. The switch was easier than I expected, and after using it for years, I’ve found that I don't really miss most of what I left behind. But there is one Google Photos feature I didn't realize I would notice until it was gone.

Immich replaced almost everything I cared about

The transition was easier than expected

Once I moved my library to Immich, I realized I wasn't giving up as much as I had expected. The basic experience of managing my photos felt familiar enough that I didn't spend weeks trying to adjust to a completely different workflow.

The biggest win for me was the automatic backup from my phone. I could take photos throughout the day and let Immich handle getting them onto my own server. I didn't have to remember to manually copy everything over, which was important because a backup system is only useful when you actually use it consistently.

I also liked having a proper timeline for browsing my library. Photos were arranged in a way that made it easy to move through different periods without dealing with a messy collection of folders and files. Albums were another part of my old workflow that I didn't have to abandon. I could still group photos for specific trips, events, or other occasions and access them from my devices.

I expected to miss Google Photos' search, but I don't

I found what I needed anyway

Search was one of the features I thought would make leaving Google Photos difficult. Google had years of data about my library, and I was used to typing a few words and getting surprisingly relevant results. I assumed I would notice the difference every time I needed to find an older picture.

That hasn't really happened. Immich's search is good enough for the way I actually use my library. If I'm trying to find photos from a particular trip, a certain person, or even something specific that appears in a picture, I can usually get there without much trouble. I don't always remember the exact date or album, so being able to search naturally is useful.

There are still situations where Google's search feels more polished, especially when I'm looking for something unusually specific. But those cases don't come up often enough for me to care. Most of the time, I can find what I'm looking for without much effort. That was a pleasant surprise. I expected search to be one of the biggest compromises of moving to Immich, but in everyday use, it simply hasn't been.

I self-hosted a Google Photos alternative with a Synology NAS — here's how it went

Build your own photo management platform with a NAS!

11
By  Rich Edmonds

The thing I actually miss is much harder to replace

Nothing quite replaces those unexpected memories

The feature I didn't expect to miss was Google Photos' Memories. I didn't think much about them while I was using the service because they were always there in the background. Every now and then, Google Photos would show me pictures from years ago, and I'd end up scrolling through them for a few minutes. I didn't realize how much I enjoyed that until those reminders disappeared.

The interesting thing is that these weren't necessarily my best photos. Sometimes they were completely ordinary pictures I had forgotten about. A random lunch, an old weekend outing, a picture of something I bought, or a moment with people I hadn't thought about in years could suddenly become interesting simply because I hadn't seen it for so long.

With Immich, I still have those photos. I can browse through them whenever I want, but I have to make the effort myself. There isn't the same feeling of being surprised by something from my own photo history. That's the part I genuinely miss. I don't miss another storage feature or a clever editing tool. I miss being reminded of moments I'd completely forgotten.

I still wouldn't switch back to Google Photos

The trade-off is worth it

Even with that one thing I miss, I have no plans to move my library back to Google Photos. Leaving it made me realize that I value having more control over where my photos live and how I manage them.

With Immich, I know exactly where my library is stored. I'm not depending on a third-party service to decide how my photos are handled, and I can manage the underlying storage myself. That gives me a level of control I didn't have before.

There is also something satisfying about knowing that my photo library isn't tied to a particular cloud service. I can change the hardware, adjust my setup, or move things around without having to rethink my entire workflow.

4 lessons I learned after switching from Google Photos to a self-hosted solution

It has gone better than expected, but with a few hurdles.

16
By  Megan Ellis

I traded convenience for control

Moving away from Google Photos taught me that not every convenience needs to be replaced. Some features are nice to have, but they aren't worth giving up control over something as personal as my photo library. Immich has changed how I manage my photos, and while I occasionally miss the little surprises from my old setup, I don't regret making the switch.

item.title: I retired my Roku stick for an Android TV box, and I'm not going back
item.itunes:title: I retired my Roku stick for an Android TV box, and I'm not going back
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When streaming media services and devices became popular, Roku was my first choice. Even with the ability to sideload other apps on Fire TV devices, I stuck with Roku boxes and sticks since they were straightforward to use, my apps synced, and I was used to the experience.

I still had a stick until retiring it in favor of an Android TV box. The number of ads on Roku is horrendous, and the platform offers no customization. I can also do a lot more with an Android/Google TV box than with the Roku OS.

Roku lacks apps and customization options

An Android TV box offers more

While Roku has more than 40,000 apps in its store, that number still pales in comparison to the number available for Android TV. Between the official Play Store, alternative stores, and Android APKs available for sideloading from GitHub and other sources, the number of apps is in the millions.

I can instantly customize the look and feel of Google TV with a few clicks using alternative launchers such as Projectivy, Arc, or Kyu. I also have access to a plethora of ways for managing my own media. Even phone apps that don't offer a TV-like viewing experience let me get things done that I can't on Roku.

The locked-down Roku operating system leaves little room for interface customization, and it definitely doesn't allow you to remove ads. I can install themes, rearrange tiles, adjust the wallpaper, or change the screensaver, but the same blocky interface with the same ad annoyances always remains; just with a theme around it.

For instance, I installed a Game of Thrones theme thinking it would revitalize my Roku, but it did nothing more than change the wallpaper and put borders around the blocky app tiles. Plus, since Fox's acquisition of Roku, ads have gotten worse, and the modern interface looks far worse than it did less than a decade ago.

Kyu Launcher
OS
Android TV
See at Google Play Store

The Roku stick experience is ad-ridden

More than the home screen is locked down

When I fire up my Roku stick and see the bombastic ads — namely the giant one on the home screen — I want to reach for the nearest custom launcher, as I mentioned above. Then I realize that Roku OS is a locked-down operating system, and I miss the openness and customizability of Android TV. Roku is locked down like Vega OS on new Fire TV sticks; there's no theming your way out of them either.

Ads don't appear only on the home screen, either. I find advertisements for shows, other apps, products, and services in banners and boxes throughout the Roku experience. Sometimes ads are animated or video, so I have to watch a full commercial — sometimes with sound — at the top, bottom, or middle of the screen while I am simply trying to flip from one app to another.

Sure, the default Google TV home screen is a mess and displays ads, but not throughout the entire experience like Roku does. Also, as I mentioned in the previous section, I can install a different launcher (whether in the app store or not) to remove ads on Android TV.

Jellyfin's Roku app just got good enough to ditch Plex

The bugs are gone too, it's safe to upgrade

2
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Roku lacks storage and functionality

I can do more with an Android TV box

A Roku stick has around 4GB of free storage, which is enough for most essential apps, plus adding some of your own. Apps are small, but streaming apps' cache can add up quickly and make the Roku less responsive. Space can also be tight if I want to install a few hundred apps for testing. I found myself uninstalling apps a lot to free up space on my Roku stick.

My Android TV box and Google TV Streamer, on the other hand, each have 32 GB of internal storage, which is enough to install a seemingly limitless number of apps and store a fair number of files locally. For instance, I can use an app like Downloader to download MP3s or other files, or send media directly from my PC or other devices using an app like LocalSend. I can then play those files directly with Kodi or VLC.

An Android box also offers more functionality. My Google TV Streamer and budget Android box include an Ethernet port for better internet and LAN reliability. That is especially helpful when using self-hosted media servers like Plex or Jellyfin. My budget Google TV box also includes a dedicated USB port for external storage so that I can set up a local media player or a self-hosted server. I can do something similar with the Streamer, using a workaround with the USB-C power port.

A Roku stick is Wi-Fi only, and there's no option to expand storage — let alone create a server from it. A Roku Ultra box has an Ethernet port and a USB port. It lets you play media files from an attached flash drive supported by Roku Media Player. However, if a file is unsupported, you can't install VLC or similar direct-play open-source apps on Roku.

Google TV Streamer 4K
Brand
Google
$100 at Amazon $100 at Best Buy

I abandoned Roku to own my media experience on Android TV

Since I have been getting into self-hosted media servers and clients more recently, and want a more customizable overall media experience, I have retired my Roku stick to my desk's junk drawer. I've realized that Roku's locked-down OS doesn't cut it for my streaming needs anymore.

I can always gift the Roku stick to a friend or family member who wants Netflix and doesn't mind obnoxious ads. Whether it's the Google TV Streamer or a budget box, Android/Google TV is a far more flexible and forgiving platform.

6 useful Fire TV Stick apps that really improve my streaming experience

Stop scrolling, start streaming.

3

item.title: I built Claude Code's workflow with a local model, and it's surprisingly close
item.itunes:title: I built Claude Code's workflow with a local model, and it's surprisingly close
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Claude Code can inspect a repository, read and edit files, run terminal commands, and check whether its changes actually work. The model plays a huge role here, of course, but much of the experience comes from the workflow built around it. I wanted to see whether I could recreate that workflow while keeping the model on my own computer. I combined Qwen 3.5 with LM Studio and Hermes Agent. I’m running the 14B model, so it’s nowhere near as good as Claude, but this setup brought me pretty close to what I had in mind, with a few limitations, of course.

item.title: I moved my most important devices off Wi-Fi, and my entire network became more reliable
item.itunes:title: I moved my most important devices off Wi-Fi, and my entire network became more reliable
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I was using Wi-Fi for far more than I should have. If a device could connect wirelessly, I usually let it, even when it sat in the same place every single day. My desktop, Apple TV, NAS, game console, and other important devices were all using the airtime for no good reason. Then I stopped treating Wi-Fi as the default.

I didn’t buy a new router, upgrade to Wi-Fi 7, or change my internet plan, yet my entire network felt more stable almost immediately.

I ran my home server on Wi-Fi for a year, and learned when Ethernet actually matters

Wired connections might be 'best' but sometimes just enough is fine

22
By  Joe Rice-Jones

I realized my most demanding devices didn’t need Wi-Fi

I was wasting Wi-Fi on stationary devices

My most demanding devices were the ones that moved the least. My Apple TV 4K sits in the same spot under the TV every day, and my Windows desktop never leaves my desk. Yet I was still letting both of them use Wi-Fi as if they needed the flexibility of a wireless connection.

That didn’t make much sense once I thought about it. These are also two of the busiest devices on my network. The Apple TV 4K regularly handles 4K streaming, while my desktop deals with large downloads, cloud backups, file transfers, local LLM updates, video calls, and plenty of other bandwidth-heavy tasks.

I was basically asking Wi-Fi to handle some of my heaviest traffic, even though both devices were sitting just a few feet away from an Ethernet connection.

So I changed the setup. I connected both devices directly to Ethernet and left Wi-Fi for the gadgets that actually benefit from it, such as phones, tablets, laptops, and smart home devices.

4K streaming became much more predictable

My Windows desktop benefited even more

The biggest difference with my Apple TV 4K wasn’t some dramatic jump in speed. It was consistency. Before switching to Ethernet, streaming was generally good, but there were occasional moments where playback took longer to start, quality dipped briefly, or the connection felt less noticeable once I wired it.

4K content now starts more predictably and stays steady even when other devices are active. I just want to press play and forget about the network.

My Windows desktop benefited even more because it does far more than stream content. Some of the bandwidth-heavy jobs can run for a long time and keep the connection busy in the background. Moving the desktop to Ethernet gave those workloads a stable wired connection instead of making them compete with other wireless devices.

I also noticed more consistent transfer speeds and fewer small network hiccups. For a machine that never leaves my desk, Wi-Fi felt unnecessary.

Fewer heavy devices make Wi-Fi feel better

My router had fewer demanding wireless clients to manage

Once I moved my Apple TV and Windows desktop to Ethernet, the biggest surprise was how much better Wi-Fi felt on everything else. My phones, tablets, laptops, and smart home devices still use the wireless network, but now they aren’t sharing it with two of the busiest devices in my setup.

I didn’t suddenly double my internet speed, but the network felt less crowded and more responsive during busy periods. That was the real win for me. Instead of trying to squeeze more performance out of Wi-Fi, I simply removed some of the traffic that never needed to be wireless in the first place.

I also started looking at the change from my router’s perspective. Wi-Fi is shared, so every wireless device is competing for airtime in some form. My desktop could be downloading a huge file while the Apple TV was streaming 4K content, all while phones, laptops, and other devices were doing their own thing.

I thought a 10GbE home networking upgrade was overkill, but it's the best upgrade I ever made

I'm here to eat humble pie and transfer data

12
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Ethernet isn’t realistic for everything

I only needed to wire two devices to notice a difference

I am not trying to turn my entire home into a wired network. Ethernet isn’t practical for everything I use. Most of the devices don’t have an Ethernet port in the first place. Besides, running cables to every corner of the house would also defeat the convenience of Wi-Fi.

For me, the better approach is selective. I keep portable and low-demand devices wireless, while stationary devices that regularly push a lot of data get Ethernet whenever possible.

What surprised me most was that I didn’t need to wire half the house to notice an improvement. I only moved my Apple TV 4K and Windows desktop to Ethernet, and that was enough to change how my network felt.

I gave Wi-Fi some breathing room

I didn’t overhaul my network, replace my router, or spend money chasing a newer Wi-Fi standard. I simply moved my Apple TV 4K and Windows desktop to Ethernet and let Wi-Fi focus on the devices that actually need to be wireless.

That small change made streaming more consistent, desktop transfers more dependable, and the rest of my wireless network less stressed.

Ethernet may feel old-school compared to Wi-Fi 7 and flashy mesh systems, but for bandwidth-heavy devices, it still makes perfect sense.

item.title: You can grab this bestselling Android tablet for $77 right now
item.itunes:title: You can grab this bestselling Android tablet for $77 right now
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The Amazon Fire HD 10 is a bestselling tablet for several reasons. It isn't for everyone, but the price will surely turn heads if you've been thinking about buying a new Android tablet. Amazon is now discounting the Fire HD 10 to just $77, which is 50% off its usual retail price of $155.

Amazon Fire HD 10

The Fire HD 10 is one of the best Fire tablets available with its large display, updated internals, and access to apps, videos, games, and more. 

See at Amazon

A perfect fit for some

Credit: Amazon

If this tablet fits your daily flow, it's worth picking up. It's just that simple. The tablet features a 10.1-inch screen, octa-core processor, 4GB of RAM, and 32GB of onboard storage. It also has a microSD card slot, so you can expand storage if needed.

Although it runs Android, it is a special version created by Amazon, which means it doesn't have access to the Google Play Store. However, Amazon has its own App Store that provides access to some of the most popular Android apps right now.

It doesn't have every app available that you'd find on the Google Play Store, but it's good enough. If you have specific needs, double-check whether your app can be downloaded to the Fire HD 10.

Beyond that, Amazon promises up to 13 hours of battery life from a single charge, which is pretty good. Charging is a bit slow at four hours from start to finish, so plan ahead. The tablet has a 5MP front-facing camera and a rear camera. The quality isn't great, but it will do the job.

And despite its lower price, this tablet charges via USB-C. Plenty of accessories are also available to make it more productive. I've used one before, and it got me by when I just needed something to listen to music, watch videos, and browse the web.

The test bench for the runs detailed below comprised of a GeForce RTX 4070 Ti Super coupled with a Ryzen 5 7600X, with 32GB of DDR5-6000 memory running with EXPO enabled.

Resident Evil Requiem

DLSS 4.5 RR brings a requiem for noisy reflections

Much of the game is characterized by dimmer lighting, matte concrete, and in a specific reflective scene that I captured under both presets, the two come quite close, barring the obvious clarity and crispiness in reflections.

Which is why I'd argue the gains become easier to spot when you put Preset F in front of reflections. Wet floors in the same dimly lit areas have more convincing color and reflection, and the lighting looks brighter and better defined. Preset D is nominally 0.7 FPS ahead, which I'd chalk up to run-to-run variance, and I am quite confident stating that there is no performance penalty. item.title: Your Docker Compose file is probably exposing services that should stay internal
item.itunes:title: Your Docker Compose file is probably exposing services that should stay internal
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I’ve been using Docker long enough to know my way around Compose files, containers, and the usual networking settings. But for years, I treated port configuration as one of those things that simply worked if the syntax was right. That changed when I started dealing with more complex setups and had to troubleshoot why services behaved differently depending on where a connection came from. I realized I had been looking at Docker networking too narrowly. The commands weren't the hard part. The missing piece was understanding what Docker was doing between the application, container, host, and network. That shift completely changed how I configure containers.

I thought Docker Port Mapping was just a number game

The left and right matter

For a long time, I treated Docker port mapping like a simple number-matching exercise. If my application used port 3000, I would usually write something like 3000:3000 in my Compose file and move on. If I wanted to use another port on my machine, I changed the first number and assumed I had changed the application's port too. That assumption caused more confusion than I realized.

I eventually understood that the two numbers in a mapping have completely different jobs. The number on the left is the port on my host, while the number on the right is the port where the application is listening inside the container. So 8080:3000 doesn't tell my application to move from 3000 to 8080. It simply gives me a way to reach the application through port 8080 on the host while the application continues using port 3000 inside the container. Once I understood that distinction, Docker port mappings stopped looking like arbitrary syntax and started making sense.

I was publishing ports that never needed to be public

Not every container needs a doorway

I used to publish ports for almost every container because it made accessing services feel easier. If I could see a port in the container's documentation, I often added it to my Compose file without thinking much about who actually needed it.

That habit became a problem when I started running multiple services together. My database, cache, and internal API didn't always need to be accessed directly from my computer. They mainly needed to talk to other containers in the same application stack.

Docker's internal networking already handles that communication. Containers can reach each other over the Docker network without every service needing a port published on the host. I was adding host mappings for connections that never needed to leave the container network.

The distinction became much clearer once I started thinking about where the traffic was going. Container-to-container communication is different from accessing a container from the host, which is different again from allowing external devices to reach it. Publishing fewer ports also meant fewer services were unnecessarily exposed on my host. My Compose files became simpler, and I had fewer things to worry about.

I started using networking sidecars for my Docker containers, and they've been a game-changer

Object-oriented orchestration is out of this world

13
By  Joe Rice-Jones

EXPOSE and localhost sometimes cause confusion

Two small concepts caused big confusion

EXPOSE and localhost are two Docker concepts that can easily create confusion, even when the rest of the networking setup is clear. The EXPOSE instruction in a Dockerfile indicates which port a containerized application is expected to listen on. It doesn't publish that port on the host or automatically make the service reachable from outside the container.

Localhost is equally important because its meaning depends on where the connection originates. Inside a container, localhost refers to that same container. It doesn't refer to the Docker host or another container running alongside it.

This distinction matters when applications communicate across containers. A service may be running correctly, while a connection still fails because the address points to the wrong network namespace.

Understanding these two concepts helps separate application configuration from Docker networking and makes connection issues much easier to troubleshoot.

Now I ask one question before publishing any Docker port

Before mapping, I think about access

Before publishing a Docker port now, I ask myself one simple question: who actually needs to access this service? That question changes how I configure a Compose stack. If a service is only part of the application's internal plumbing, I don't automatically give it a host-facing port. If I need to access it during development, I consider whether that access is temporary or something the setup genuinely requires.

I also consider each service's role before adding another mapping. A web application may need direct access, while a database, cache, or internal worker may not. Keeping those decisions intentional prevents my Compose files from filling up with ports that exist simply because they were convenient at the time. This approach has made my Docker configurations easier to maintain. Instead of publishing ports by habit, I now treat every mapping as a deliberate networking decision with a specific reason behind it.

I save $100 every month with these 7 docker containers in my home lab

I stopped paying for various cloud services and replaced them with Docker containers that give me more control, and privacy.

By  Yash Patel

The biggest lesson wasn't about ports

Docker made me realize that configuration and networking are more connected than they first appear. A setup can work perfectly while still hiding assumptions that become painful later. Once I started paying attention to how services communicate, many of those confusing moments became easier to reason about. The biggest improvement wasn't learning another Docker command. It was developing a better mental model of what was happening underneath the containers. That understanding has stayed useful far beyond port mappings.

I’ve been using Docker long enough to know my way around Compose files, containers, and the usual networking settings. But for years, I treated port configuration as one of those things that simply worked if the syntax was right. That changed when I started dealing with more complex setups and had to troubleshoot why services behaved differently depending on where a connection came from. I realized I had been looking at Docker networking too narrowly. The commands weren't the hard part. The missing piece was understanding what Docker was doing between the application, container, host, and network. That shift completely changed how I configure containers.

I thought Docker Port Mapping was just a number game

The left and right matter

For a long time, I treated Docker port mapping like a simple number-matching exercise. If my application used port 3000, I would usually write something like 3000:3000 in my Compose file and move on. If I wanted to use another port on my machine, I changed the first number and assumed I had changed the application's port too. That assumption caused more confusion than I realized.

I eventually understood that the two numbers in a mapping have completely different jobs. The number on the left is the port on my host, while the number on the right is the port where the application is listening inside the container. So 8080:3000 doesn't tell my application to move from 3000 to 8080. It simply gives me a way to reach the application through port 8080 on the host while the application continues using port 3000 inside the container. Once I understood that distinction, Docker port mappings stopped looking like arbitrary syntax and started making sense.

I was publishing ports that never needed to be public

Not every container needs a doorway

I used to publish ports for almost every container because it made accessing services feel easier. If I could see a port in the container's documentation, I often added it to my Compose file without thinking much about who actually needed it.

That habit became a problem when I started running multiple services together. My database, cache, and internal API didn't always need to be accessed directly from my computer. They mainly needed to talk to other containers in the same application stack.

Docker's internal networking already handles that communication. Containers can reach each other over the Docker network without every service needing a port published on the host. I was adding host mappings for connections that never needed to leave the container network.

The distinction became much clearer once I started thinking about where the traffic was going. Container-to-container communication is different from accessing a container from the host, which is different again from allowing external devices to reach it. Publishing fewer ports also meant fewer services were unnecessarily exposed on my host. My Compose files became simpler, and I had fewer things to worry about.

I started using networking sidecars for my Docker containers, and they've been a game-changer

Object-oriented orchestration is out of this world

13
By  Joe Rice-Jones

EXPOSE and localhost sometimes cause confusion

Two small concepts caused big confusion

EXPOSE and localhost are two Docker concepts that can easily create confusion, even when the rest of the networking setup is clear. The EXPOSE instruction in a Dockerfile indicates which port a containerized application is expected to listen on. It doesn't publish that port on the host or automatically make the service reachable from outside the container.

Localhost is equally important because its meaning depends on where the connection originates. Inside a container, localhost refers to that same container. It doesn't refer to the Docker host or another container running alongside it.

This distinction matters when applications communicate across containers. A service may be running correctly, while a connection still fails because the address points to the wrong network namespace.

Understanding these two concepts helps separate application configuration from Docker networking and makes connection issues much easier to troubleshoot.

Now I ask one question before publishing any Docker port

Before mapping, I think about access

Before publishing a Docker port now, I ask myself one simple question: who actually needs to access this service? That question changes how I configure a Compose stack. If a service is only part of the application's internal plumbing, I don't automatically give it a host-facing port. If I need to access it during development, I consider whether that access is temporary or something the setup genuinely requires.

I also consider each service's role before adding another mapping. A web application may need direct access, while a database, cache, or internal worker may not. Keeping those decisions intentional prevents my Compose files from filling up with ports that exist simply because they were convenient at the time. This approach has made my Docker configurations easier to maintain. Instead of publishing ports by habit, I now treat every mapping as a deliberate networking decision with a specific reason behind it.

The biggest lesson wasn't about ports

Docker made me realize that configuration and networking are more connected than they first appear. A setup can work perfectly while still hiding assumptions that become painful later. Once I started paying attention to how services communicate, many of those confusing moments became easier to reason about. The biggest improvement wasn't learning another Docker command. It was developing a better mental model of what was happening underneath the containers. That understanding has stayed useful far beyond port mappings.

item.title: PLA and PETG win at different jobs, and matching the material to the part saved me hundreds in failed prints
item.itunes:title: PLA and PETG win at different jobs, and matching the material to the part saved me hundreds in failed prints
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I began my 3D printing journey, I pretty much stuck to PLA alone for my models. In all fairness, that turned out to be the right call, since my early days as a 3D printing enthusiast were spent creating novelty prints, cool miniature models, and decorative accessories. However, things took a turn for the worse when I tried using PLA for functional models, as my painstakingly-printed STL files would become unusable anytime they got exposed to harsh conditions.

That’s when I decided to go down the PETG route, and despite some requiring a handful of slicer optimizations, this filament worked pretty darn well with prints that would get exposed to structural stress during normal usage. Unfortunately, PETG had its own caveats when I tried using it for simple prototypes, D&D minis, and other simple models that needed sharper details. That’s when I realized that both filaments were meant for completely different use cases, and that becoming a staunch member of either camp and disregarding the other would just cause complications in my 3D printed projects.

Your multi-color prints don't have to waste filament, and the fix is simpler than you'd expect

Multi-color 3D printing doesn’t always involve wasted filament

5
By  Ayush Pande

I stick to PLA for easy-to-print models with finer details

It’s also pretty effective for prototyping new revisions of custom models

Starting with the cheapest and most accessible 3D printing filament, PLA is my go-to option for simple models that won’t get exposed to a lot of heat, UV light, or physical stress during day-to-day tasks. Novelty prints are a good example, and everything from quirky desk organizers to articulated toys looks great on PLA. Likewise, PLA doesn’t lose a lot of detail when it’s printed, making it a solid option for turning virtual STL files into tangible models with smooth edges.

Of course, it can’t rival the likes of full-on resin printers when it comes to capturing details. But if I had to print cool-looking miniatures for my tabletop game campaigns, PLA is far easier to use than resin or its FDM sibling filaments. PLA filament rolls also have fairly minimal stringing and are fairly slow at absorbing moisture, so I don’t need to dry them for hours to prevent failed prints.

It’s also great for creating prototypes of decorative CAD models, and it’s my filament of choice when I need to calibrate new printers (or even old ones after loading them with a third-party firmware). Likewise, it’s just as effective for cosplay props, and as long as I don’t expose them to direct sunlight or mechanical forces, it can even serve decently well for cheap prints with moving parts.

That said, I’d never use PLA for prints that get exposed to daily wear

Despite its easy-to-use nature, PLA is downright terrible for functional prints. For one, it starts to soften at the 55–65 °C mark, meaning it’s not something I can use to design dashboard accessories, GPU support brackets, gardening prints, or even decorative items I can put on a windowsill.

Worse still, PLA creeps under load, and if I use it for anything that has sustained pressure from hanging objects or tight screws, it’s bound to snap off in a matter of weeks. That’s where PETG comes into the equation…

But PETG is superior for anything with functional parts

It’s a lot safer to use in harsher environments than PLA

When it comes to utility objects that need more durability than what PLA can offer, I tend to stick to PETG for the most part. Unlike PLA, PETG can handle physical stress a lot better, so it’s good for cantilevers, L-shaped arms, and other snap-fits that encounter constant mechanical load. It also handles higher temperatures much better than PLA, which is why it serves as a solid option for making laptop stands, SBC cases, and even home lab racks.

I also rely on PETG for tripod mods, garden accessories, support brackets, and other prints that get exposed to sunlight and/or light rain. Car accessories, too, benefit from the PETG treatment, and I’ve got different spell slot sliders, HP counters, initiative trackers, and other functional D&D prints created from this robust filament. On the PC front, I’ve used PETG for my GPU’s anti-sag support bracket, headphone stand, USB holders, drive caddies, and (most importantly) cable management channels, and I haven’t had any issues with these prints even after months of dedicated use.

Vanity models, however, are a completely different story altogether

Although I prefer PETG for functional prints, I’d rather not use it for models where aesthetics matter above all else. It’s not as good as PLA for preserving details, and truth be told, I’m not too fond of the glossy finish that PETG models tend to have, especially since it highlights all the tiny imperfections in my prints.

PETG is also rather hygroscopic, so I need a dedicated drying machine to store unused rolls or risk letting them waste away in my humid backwater town. I had to fine-tune the PETG profiles on all my printers to get the bed adhesion and oozing problems sorted out, something that I never had to worry about with PLA. Stringing is more prominent on PETG prints, so they require more post-processing as well. It definitely needs more attention than the set-and-forget PLA, but it’s undoubtedly better for models that can get worn out by everyday use.

7 Things I wish I knew before building my 3D printed headphones

Trading frustration for solvable problems

By  Chandraveer Mathur

Splitting my 3D printing escapades between PLA and PETG worked in my favor

Despite wanting to stay with a single filament in my early 3D printing days, both PLA and PETG have become irreplaceable in my home lab. PLA handles all the novelty models, prototypes, and even random benchy instances I use to calibrate fresh 3D printer settings, while PETG is responsible for functional prints and models that I’d rather not replace every other week because they broke off under stress or became warped because I left them in direct sunlight.

item.title: I stopped using Jellyfin for everything after discovering what VLC can actually do
item.itunes:title: I stopped using Jellyfin for everything after discovering what VLC can actually do
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've been using VLC for years now, and despite the occasional flings with other media players like PotPlayer and mpv, I've always found myself coming back to VLC, all for the right reasons. After a decade of constant use, I'd been under the impression that I knew all it was capable of.

And yet, I'd somehow overlooked one of its most interesting tricks: VLC can stream media, too. It's not particularly surprising, though; I did get caught off guard by just how much control VLC let me have once I stopped treating it like a simple media player.

Over the past week, I've used VLC to send media across my network, transcode on the fly, and even exposed streaming options that feel way too sophisticated for something buried inside a media player that hasn't changed its interface in over a decade.

VLC can stream my media instead of just playing it

The "Stream" button has been a game-changer

VLC's Media > Stream option makes things much more interesting than just playing a regular local video. Instead of simply opening a local video and decoding it on your PC, VLC can take that media and send it somewhere else on your local network.

Sure, I can just add a new movie to my Jellyfin library any time, but when a new video comes up from my Google Drive, or when I connect my external HDD for the occasional home video watch party, it's much easier to stream the videos straight from VLC to the living room TV.

VLC acts as the source, which lets my PC do all the heavy lifting while the TVs in the den or the living room just receive the resulting stream with no added loads, which bypasses the whole media-server commitment.

It's been particularly useful when streaming from my laptop to my TV during watch parties, since I can select exactly which video to play on the big screen at a moment's notice without my guests having to navigate the Wholphin app on the TV. Plus, this way, I don't have to remember deleting the home video library from my Jellyfin server, either. If you just need one computer to serve one piece of media to another device, VLC can get remarkably close to the point before "simple" starts becoming a technical project.

6 lessons I learned after ditching Plex for Jellyfin on my NAS

A self-hosted setup that finally feels mine

20
By  Karandeep Singh

Then I found VLC could do even more

So much more than just a media player

Once I started looking beyond VLC's basic streaming setup, I realized that VLC can actually transcode the media while I share it over my network. It allows me to change the format, codec, bitrate, resolution, and other parameters before the receiving device gets it. That's how I've made my old laptop effectively become a tiny, somewhat overqualified broadcast station.

There's no guarantee that the device receiving the stream will understand the file you started with. I don't have to convert my entire library beforehand, since VLC can perform that conversion as the stream is produced. A video that refuses to play natively on the destination can therefore become something considerably more agreeable, without creating another copy of the original file.

It's not every day I can say I've been learning new things about a software I've been using for years now, but VLC's Profile Editor has had me doing exactly that. Its options have revealed just how much more flexible the streaming engine can be. Users can define inputs, outputs, transcoding parameters, network destinations, and other settings in a way that can be saved and repeated.
